"question-a5dc4674-bf70-593d-b79c-9ae4e2518f41"] [17592186199518 :tutorial/content "Recall that the statement "$A$ and $B$", represented symbolically as $A \land B,$ is true if $A$ is true *and* $B$ is true. Otherwise, it is false.

We can represent all possible permutations of the truth values of $A$ and $B$ and the subsequent truth values of $A\land B$ using a **truth table**:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A \land B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

Each row of the truth table contains an input for $A,$ an input for $B,$ and the corresponding output for $A \land B.$

- The first row says that if $A$ is true and $B$ is true, then $A \land B$ is true.

- The second row says that if $A$ is true and $B$ is false, then $A \land B$ is false.

- The third row says that if $A$ is false and $B$ is true, then $A \land B$ is false.

- The fourth row says that if $A$ is false and $B$ is false, then $A \land B$ is false."] [17592186199600 :tutorial/content "The statement "$A$ or $B$," represented symbolically as $A \lor B,$ is true if $A$ is true, or $B$ is true, or both $A$ and $B$ are true. Otherwise, it is false. 

The corresponding truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A \lor B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

As we'll see, truth tables provide a convenient way to determine the truth values of complex logical statements. They can also be used to prove some mathematical theorems!"] [17592186199601 :tutorial/content "Consider the following statement:

$$
A \land (B\lor A)
$$

 

We can use a truth table to calculate the truth values of this statement given all possible permutations of the truth values of $A$ and $B.$

First, we complete a truth table for the part in parentheses, $B \lor A.$  The statement $B \lor A$ is true if either $A$ is true, $B$ is true, or both $A$ and $B$ are true.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

Next, we add a new column for $A \land (B\lor A).$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |

To fill in the rows, we consider the truth values of $A$ and $(B\lor A)$ and use this to determine the truth value of $A \land (B\lor A)$ in each case.

- Consider the first row. Since $A$ is true and $(B\lor A)$ is true, their conjunction $A \land (B\lor A)$ is *true*:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |

- Next, consider the second row. Since $A$ is true and $(B\lor A)$ is true, their conjunction $A \land (B\lor A)$ is *true*:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |

- Now, consider the third row. Since $A$ is false and $(B\lor A)$ is true, their conjunction $A \land (B\lor A)$ is *false*:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |

- Finally, consider the fourth row. Since $A$ is false and $(B\lor A)$ is false, their conjunction $A \land (B\lor A)$ is *false*:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |

The completed truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |"] [17592186199519 :tutorial/content "Two statements are **logically equivalent** if they have identical truth tables. 

A trivial logical equivalence is that every statement is logically equivalent to itself. We write this as follows:

$$
P \equiv P
$$

To prove this, we can use a truth table.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,P\,$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

Since $P$ and $P$ have identical truth values, they're logically equivalent.

Another trivial equivalence is that the conjunction of a statement with itself is equivalent to the original statement.

$$
P \land P \equiv P
$$

For example, the compound statement "$x=3$ and $x=3$" is logically equivalent to "$x=3$", which matches our intuition. 

Again, we can prove the general result using a truth table.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,P\,$ | $\,P \land P\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

The statements $P$ and $P\land P$ are logically equivalent since they have identical truth values. 

We also have the following logical equivalence for the disjunction of $P$ with itself.

$$
P \lor P \equiv P
$$

We can justify this result using a truth table. 

| $\,P\,$ | $\,P\,$ | $\,P \lor P\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

The statements $P$ and $P\lor P$ are logically equivalent since they have identical truth values. 

Collectively, the results

$$
P\land P \equiv P ,\qquad P\lor P \equiv P
$$

are known as the **idempotent laws.**"] [17592186198512 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-83b5db67-0cfd-59f0-8254-1d32998685fc" :question/id #uuid "83b5db67-0cfd-59f0-8254-1d32998685fc"] ["question-83b5db67-0cfd-59f0-8254-1d32998685fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-47984"] ["question-83b5db67-0cfd-59f0-8254-1d32998685fc" :question/problem "Find the derivative of $y=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{3}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.$"] ["question-83b5db67-0cfd-59f0-8254-1d32998685fc" :question/worked-solution "We know that $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Applying this formula, we have

First, we compute the derivative, using the fact that $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)={sec}^{2}⁡x$ and $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x)=6.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =6-{sec}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =6-{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6-{(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})})}^{2} \\  & =6-{(\frac{1}{1/2})}^{2} \\  & =6-4 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change is $2.$"] ["question-9b9f5ad2-fc37-5cb1-8895-57f56e806362" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-847db2ec-c888-5238-a1ba-407a230ec903" :answer-field/id #uuid "847db2ec-c888-5238-a1ba-407a230ec903"] ["answer-4316991d-1d98-5261-b089-c06f2c337224" :answer/id #uuid "4316991d-1d98-5261-b089-c06f2c337224"] ["answer-4316991d-1d98-5261-b089-c06f2c337224" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-4316991d-1d98-5261-b089-c06f2c337224" :answer/value "2"] ["answer-field-847db2ec-c888-5238-a1ba-407a230ec903" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-847db2ec-c888-5238-a1ba-407a230ec903" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-847db2ec-c888-5238-a1ba-407a230ec903" :answer-field/correct "answer-4316991d-1d98-5261-b089-c06f2c337224"] ["answer-field-847db2ec-c888-5238-a1ba-407a230ec903" :answer-field/choices "answer-4316991d-1d98-5261-b089-c06f2c337224"] ["question-9b9f5ad2-fc37-5cb1-8895-57f56e806362" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-847db2ec-c888-5238-a1ba-407a230ec903"] [17592186059676 :knowledge-point/questions "question-9b9f5ad2-fc37-5cb1-8895-57f56e806362"] ["question-75deedc5-439f-5c0b-9ed9-ea7f29313f69" :question/id #uuid "75deedc5-439f-5c0b-9ed9-ea7f29313f69"] ["question-75deedc5-439f-5c0b-9ed9-ea7f29313f69" :question/math-academy-id "q-341826"] ["question-75deedc5-439f-5c0b-9ed9-ea7f29313f69" :question/problem "Calculate the instantaneous rate of change of the function $f(x)=4x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ when $x=0.$

We see that ${f}^{′}(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (-5,4),$ and ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at $x=0.$ Therefore, the candidates are $x=-5,0,4.$

**Step 2**: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

The function is made up of $1$ trapezoid and $2$ triangles. Let's add the areas bounded by these shapes to our diagram:

![](images/a8/a8bff8783c0e536cd0e3c475a8fca87a9861a1e1f0ca7f2833ca9c434da2426d.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =1 \\ f(0) & =f(4)+{\int }_{4}^{0}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =f(4)-{\int }_{0}^{4}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =1-(-8) \\  & =1+8 \\  & =9 \\ f(-5) & =f(4)+{\int }_{4}^{-5}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =f(4)-{\int }_{-5}^{4}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =1-(9+2-8) \\  & =1-3 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates. 

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have

$$
{f}_{\text{min}}=min\{1,9,-2\}=-2.
$$

The joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given above, while the marginal mass functions for these variables are shown below.

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $P(X=0,Y=2)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=2)$

II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent"] ["question-d05ba4df-d0b9-5ab9-9679-a4617e87b3ef" :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=2)=f(0,2)=0.15.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=2)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2)=0.6\cdot 0.25=0.15.\,✓
$$

- Statement II is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,4) & =0.45=0.6\cdot 0.75={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(4) & ✓ \\ f(1,2) & =0.1=0.4\cdot 0.25={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2) & ✓ \\ f(1,4) & =0.3=0.4\cdot 0.75={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(4) & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""] ["question-d05ba4df-d0b9-5ab9-9679-a4617e87b3ef" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] Which of the following statements are true?

I. $P(X=0,Y=1)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=1)$

II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent"] ["question-3efec416-c341-5cd9-8d7e-9c91c7f8fc1f" :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statements I and II are false. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=1)=f(0,1)=0.32.$ However, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=1)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1)=0.7\cdot 0.6=0.42.\,\times
$$

Therefore, 

$$
P(X=0,Y=1)\ne P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=1),
$$

and $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""] ["question-3efec416-c341-5cd9-8d7e-9c91c7f8fc1f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=0)=f(0,0)=0.07.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0)=0.35\cdot 0.2=0.07.\,✓
$$

- Statement II is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1) & =0.28=0.35\cdot 0.8={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓ \\ f(1,0) & =0.13=0.65\cdot 0.2={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) & ✓ \\ f(1,1) & =0.52=0.65\cdot 0.8={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""] ["question-5ad1bec0-7cb2-5524-90ce-c8dd7afd9873" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.11$ | $0.44$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.09$ | $0.36$ |

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $P(X=0,Y=1)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=1)$

II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent"] ["question-5dd8077d-1403-5bd2-b29d-34936c801dde" :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Computing the marginal probability mass functions for  $X$ and $Y,$ we obtain the following:

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.11$ | $0.44$ | $0.55$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.09$ | $0.36$ | $0.45$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.2$ | $0.8$ | $1$ |

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=1)=f(0,1)=0.11.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=1)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1)=0.55\cdot 0.2=0.11.\,✓
$$

- Statement II is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2) & =0.44=0.55\cdot 0.8={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2) & ✓ \\ f(1,1) & =0.09=0.45\cdot 0.2={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓ \\ f(1,2) & =0.36=0.45\cdot 0.8={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2) & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""] ["question-5dd8077d-1403-5bd2-b29d-34936c801dde" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] | --- | --- | --- |

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $P(X=3,Y=2)=P(X=3)\cdot P(Y=2)$

II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent"] ["question-86447238-489f-5596-b009-12655e2594dd" :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if

$$

 
for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Computing the marginal probability mass functions for  $X$ and $Y,$ we obtain the following:

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ | $0.8$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.8$ | $0.2$ | $1$ |

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statements I and II are false. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=3,Y=2)=f(3,2)=0.1.$ However, 

$$
P(X=3)\cdot P(Y=2)={f}_{X}(3)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2)=0.2\cdot 0.8=0.16.\,\times
$$

Therefore, 

$$
P(X=3,Y=2)\ne P(X=3)\cdot P(Y=2),
$$

and $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of those listed.""] ["question-86447238-489f-5596-b009-12655e2594dd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-6f0201d6-c736-51e8-8b5c-a5fa2133c2b7" :question/worked-solution "Let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).$

![](images/52/52817b9c0ede04e8e920de8a52ebe025916f314cc937097c7fb91ea612e18f1b.png)

The function is not defined for $x\le -1.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)=\text{DNE}.
$$

However, the function is defined for $x>-1.$ Moreover,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)=-\infty .
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are not equal, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)=\text{DNE}.
$$"] ["question-6f0201d6-c736-51e8-8b5c-a5fa2133c2b7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bec4ef46-c3c9-5b5f-b667-e3c769648f01" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-e645c316-71e4-58c2-8dda-54dfd003d3ee" :question/math-academy-id "q-90968"] ["question-e645c316-71e4-58c2-8dda-54dfd003d3ee" :question/problem "What is the range of the function $f(x)=-{x}^{2}+6x-8?$"] ["question-e645c316-71e4-58c2-8dda-54dfd003d3ee" :question/worked-solution "The given parabola is written in standard form,

$$
y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c,
$$

with $a=-1<0,$ $b=6,$ and $c=-8.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The $x$-coordinate of the vertex is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{6}{2\cdot (-1)}=3.
$$

Now, we substitute $x=3$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-{x}^{2}+6x-8 \\  & =-(3)^{2}+6(3)-8 \\  & =-9+18-8 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(3,1),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,1].$

$f(x)=-3(x+1)^{2}-7?$"] ["question-8a71e9cb-8bb6-5c17-8cab-a2b0b8515a29" :question/worked-solution "The parabola is written in vertex form, 

$$
y=a(x-h)^{2}+k,
$$

where $a$ is the leading coefficient and $(h,k)$ is the vertex. 

- Since $h=-1$ and $k=-7,$ the vertex is $(-1,-7).$

- Since $a=-3<0,$ the parabola opens downwards.

Because the parabola opens downwards, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output. 

Therefore, the range is $(-\infty ,-7].$

The corresponding diagram is shown below.

:question/problem "Find the range of the function $f(x)=-(x+7)(x+9).$

{{field-1}}
$<f(x)$
{{field-2}}{{field-3}}"] ["question-fb786a48-6efc-557e-bdac-ba3e5bfceb11" :question/worked-solution "The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-1<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-9$ and ${x}_{2}=-7,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-9-7}{2}=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=-8$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(x+7)(x+9) \\  & =-(-8+7)(-8+9) \\  & =-(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(-8,1),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,1],$ i.e. $-\infty <f(x)\le 1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{5-{x}^{4}}{6{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6}{x}^{-2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-20{x}^{-5} \\  & =-\frac{20}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-224e49e4-5633-5d71-8ad0-69cc905bfd6e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e6989b96-6453-5959-889b-dc271201d958" :answer-field/id #uuid {{field-1}}."] ["question-30675b2a-1249-5c56-916f-1fdddcd8a518" :question/worked-solution "Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3x) \\  & =x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3) \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-30675b2a-1249-5c56-916f-1fdddcd8a518" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-fae03ebe-384c-56a0-b28b-7e7a4779e500" :answer-field/id #uuid "fae03ebe-384c-56a0-b28b-7e7a4779e500"] ["answer-d8882614-1542-5cb1-8585-441d502aa822" :answer/id #uuid "d8882614-1542-5cb1-8585-441d502aa822"] ["answer-d8882614-1542-5cb1-8585-441d502aa822" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d8882614-1542-5cb1-8585-441d502aa822" :answer/value "-\cos x"] ["answer-field-fae03ebe-384c-56a0-b28b-7e7a4779e500" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-fae03ebe-384c-56a0-b28b-7e7a4779e500" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-fae03ebe-384c-56a0-b28b-7e7a4779e500" :answer-field/correct "answer-d8882614-1542-5cb1-8585-441d502aa822"] ["answer-field-fae03ebe-384c-56a0-b28b-7e7a4779e500" :answer-field/choices "answer-d8882614-1542-5cb1-8585-441d502aa822"] ["question-30675b2a-1249-5c56-916f-1fdddcd8a518" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-fae03ebe-384c-56a0-b28b-7e7a4779e500"] [17592186059679 :knowledge-point/questions "question-30675b2a-1249-5c56-916f-1fdddcd8a518"] [17592186060897 :tutorial/content "The **second derivative**  is the derivative of a function's first derivative. It is written as $f''(x).$

To calculate the second derivative of a function $f(x)$, we first need to calculate the first derivative $f'(x).$ After that, we calculate the derivative of $f'(x).$ So using prime $\left('\right)$ notation, we can define the second derivative of a function $f(x)$ as

$$
f''(x) = (f'(x))'.
$$

Let's try it out with the function $f(x) = 4x^2 + 3x.$ The first derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =(4{x}^{2}+3x)^{′} \\  & =4(2)x+3 \\  & =8x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the derivative of $f'(x)$ to give us $f''(x).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =({f}^{′}(x))^{′} \\  & =(8x+3)^{′} \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the second derivative of $f(x)$ is $8.$"] [17592186060899 :tutorial/content "To calculate the third derivative of the function $f(x)=2x^4+3x,$ we need to differentiate it three times.

Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{4}+3x) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{4-1}+1\cdot 3{x}^{1-1} \\ \text{ } & =8{x}^{3}+3{x}^{0} \\  & =8{x}^{3}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{3}+3) \\  & =8\cdot 3{x}^{3-1}+0 \\ \text{ } & =24{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(24{x}^{2}) \\  & =24\cdot 2{x}^{2-1} \\ \text{ } & =48x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third derivative of $f(x)$ is $f'''(x)=48x.$ 

Using Leibniz notation, the third derivative of a function $f(x)$ can also be written as

$$
f'''(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(f(x))\right)\right)=\dfrac {\textrm d^3}{\textrm d x^3}f(x).
$$

In general, if we want to calculate the $n$-th order derivative of a function, we need to differentiate it $n$ times:

$$
f^{(n)}(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d^n}{\textrm d x^n}f(x).
$$

**Note**: The parenthesis in the superscript of $f^{(n)}(x)$ means that it is the the $n$-th derivative of $f(x).$ This is to distinguish it from $f^n(x)$ with no parenthesis, which indicates the $n$-th power of $f(x).$"] [17592186059952 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0] ["question-822263d6-7f5d-5a37-a89e-f93c0b6eb7bf" :question/id #uuid "822263d6-7f5d-5a37-a89e-f93c0b6eb7bf"] ["question-822263d6-7f5d-5a37-a89e-f93c0b6eb7bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-39499"] ["question-822263d6-7f5d-5a37-a89e-f93c0b6eb7bf" :question/problem "![](images/ad/ad5f193a1ff21e03659789473a6e4918b6dd7ba25cd9db4e6fc0f729d0481391.png)

"![](images/74/7471044234ec20534f33abb45d26db3c0a2876bed0fcc73844d1867b354491c0.png)

Which of the following statements are true for the graph shown above?

I. $f(x)\to 2$ as $x\to -\infty$

II. $f(x)\to 1$ as $x\to \infty$

III. $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to -\infty$"] ["question-994cad67-228c-54a3-8cec-2145c453420a" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement one-by-one.

- On the left of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets more and more negative, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $2.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 2\,\text{as}\,x\to -\infty
$$

Therefore, statement I is true while statement III is false.

- On the right of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets larger and larger, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $1.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty
$$

Therefore, statement II is true.

As a result, the correct answer is "I and II only"."] ["question-994cad67-228c-54a3-8cec-2145c453420a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] "![](images/c1/c12deadd41a9c2853d0d2d50ba5c19ac6ca13012d7672941c92fa5e6cc5df642.png)

Which of the following statements are true for the graph shown above?

I. $y=-1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$

II. $y=1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$

III. $y=2$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$"] ["question-eab5bcd3-8a73-5188-a5f4-a81be3ecb0f7" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement one-by-one.

- On the right of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets larger and larger, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $1.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty
$$

This means that $y=1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x).$ Therefore, statement II is true.

- On the left of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets more and more negative, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $2.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 2\,\text{as}\,x\to -\infty .
$$

This means that $y=2$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x).$ Therefore, III is also true.

- The horizontal asymptotes of $f(x)$ are $y=1$ and $y=2.$ The line $y=-1$ is not a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ because the function does not level off to $-1$ on the right nor on the left. Therefore, I is false.

As a result, the correct answer is "II and III only"."] ["question-eab5bcd3-8a73-5188-a5f4-a81be3ecb0f7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] (*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)"] ["question-1d85a230-c47c-5ffa-b563-dedfdd86c871" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the function is a product of $3$ linear binomials, so this function is a cubic function. Moreover, it is a negative cubic because if we were to expand the parentheses, the coefficient of the ${x}^{3}$ term would be negative:

$$
-3(x+2)(x+1)(x-1)=-3x\cdot x\cdot x+⋯=-3{x}^{3}+⋯
$$

The equation is given in the factored form. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the roots are  $x=-2,$ $x=-1,$ and $x=1.$ 

We now find the $y$-intercept of the curve by plugging the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-3(0+2)(0+1)(0-1) \\  & =-3(2)(1)(-1) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an $\text{S}$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=-2,-1,1$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=6,$ as follows:

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)"] ["question-2c01baff-ab5f-57ff-be23-ce994353bbde" :question/worked-solution "First, we notice that the function is a negative cubic curve because the coefficient of ${x}^{3}$ is negative.

We are told that $x=2$ is a root of $f(x),$ which means that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ So, to find the other roots of $f(x)$ we use synthetic division to divide $f(x)$ by $(x-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 2 & -1 & 7 & -14 & 8 \\  &  & -2 & 10 & -8 \\  & -1 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

We obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-2)(-{x}^{2}+5x-4) \\  & =-(x-2)({x}^{2}-5x+4) \\  & =-(x-2)(x-1)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to zero, we find that the other roots of $f(x)$ are $x=1$ and $x=4.$ 

Now, let's find the $y$-intercept. To do that, we substitute $x=0,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0-2)(0-1)(0-4) \\  & =-(-2)(-1)(-4) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an $S$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=1,2,4$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=8,$ as follows:

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)"] ["question-1fbfa8ab-6879-57fc-b2d0-196f095281bf" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that the function is a positive cubic curve because the coefficient of ${x}^{3}$ is positive.

We are told that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so to find the other roots of $f(x)$ we use synthetic division to divide $f(x)$ by  $(x+3):$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & -9 & -18 \\  &  & -3 & 3 & 18 \\  & 1 & -1 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

We obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+3)({x}^{2}-x-6) \\  & =(x+3)(x+2)(x-3),\end{aligned}
$$

so the roots of $f(x)$ are $x=-3,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=3.$ 

Now, let's find the $y$-intercept. To do that, we substitute $x=0,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(0+3)(0+2)(0-3) \\  & =(3)(2)(-3) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an inverted $\text{S}$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=-3,-2,3$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=-18,$ as follows:

["question-3d714d9e-2644-5dbb-a0ee-6c22b2b05b9a" :question/problem "Given the statement

$$
P:2\text{ divides }8
$$

 
which of the following represents the statement $¬P?$"] ["question-3d714d9e-2644-5dbb-a0ee-6c22b2b05b9a" :question/worked-solution "The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

$$
¬P:\text{It is not true that }2\text{ divides }8,
$$

 

In other words, $2$ does *not* divide $8.$ Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$$
¬P:2\text{ does }\text{not}\text{ divide }8.
$$

Note that $P$ is **true,** while $¬P$ is **false.**"] ["question-3d714d9e-2644-5dbb-a0ee-6c22b2b05b9a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] - The negation of the *true* statement "$4$ is divisible by $2$" is the *false* statement "$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$"

- The negation of the *false* statement "$5$ is even" is the *true* statement "$5$ is odd."

We can express negations using the symbol "$\neg$". The negation of $A$ is denoted $\neg A,$ and has the opposite truth values as $A{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

We can negate compound statements as well. For example, the statement $\neg (A \land B)$ has the opposite truth values as the statement $A \land B{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, \neg (A \land B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |"] [17592186153427 :tutorial/content "When we have two negations in a row, we can cancel them out.

- For example, $\neg (\neg A)$ can be simplified to $A.$

- Likewise, $\neg (\neg (A \land B))$ can be simplified to $A \land B.$

To understand why negations cancel with each other, consider the following statement: 

$4$ is divisible by $2.$

The negation of this statement is 

$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$

If we negate again, we get back the original sentence: 

$4$ divisible by $2.$

So, if we negate a statement twice, we end up with the original statement.

More formally, we can prove that $\neg (\neg A) \equiv A$ using a truth table.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ | $\,\neg(\neg A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |

Since $A$ and $\neg(\neg A)$ have the same truth values, they are logically equivalent."] [17592186152374 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-0f13da88-9214-5888-9868-a4b7f8edacdd" :question/id #uuid "0f13da88-9214-5888-9868-a4b7f8edacdd"] ["question-0f13da88-9214-5888-9868-a4b7f8edacdd" :question/math-academy-id "q-72721"] ["question-0f13da88-9214-5888-9868-a4b7f8edacdd" :question/problem "Suppose $B$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(B)=-21.$ The matrix $C$ is obtained from $B$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{4}$ (switching the first and the fourth rows). ["question-a1f0bc2a-d097-538a-b002-360896d3c91f" :question/worked-solution "First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

$$

"question-d7915d65-a649-5e77-8661-8aa533c4bd16"] [17592186121020 :tutorial/content "Remember the following three standard elementary row operations: 

  I. Swapping two rows

  II. Multiplying a row by a non-zero number

  III. Adding a multiple of one row to another row

Of these three elementary row operations, only III (adding a multiple of one row to another row) *preserves* the determinant. The other two operations, switching two rows or multiplying a row by a non-zero number, *change* the determinant.

To demonstrate, let's consider the matrix ![](images/fa/fa51d7c585db408c47e8640ae839c1a3bbf94e2b0097e1ade511e5773461f1e8.svg) Taking the determinant, we have
![](images/bc/bcf5c5dc9f5b7ed3849e719665f802040cf51e3334ae99e25ea7648cbb0f6134.svg)

If we swap the two rows, we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4 \\  & =2 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, if we multiply top row by ${\color{red}2},$ then we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

However, if we add twice the top row to the bottom row, then we get the same determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3+2\cdot 1 & 4+2\cdot 2\end{vmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot 8-2\cdot 5 \\  & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186121061 :tutorial/content "Let's check what happens if we multiply the entire matrix (not only one row) by a number. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3\cdot 1 & 3\cdot 2 \\ 3\cdot 3 & 3\cdot 4\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 9 & 12\end{vmatrix} & =3\cdot 12-6\cdot 9=-18\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

![](images/fe/fe02091dde43a8a2405f6b588f619bc9fa3f54b31ac8a1ac39d318761f00cc3e.svg)

The above is equivalent to multiplying both rows of the matrix by $3$. Multiplying the first row scales the determinant by $3$, and then multiplying the second row scales it by $3$ once more.

In general, multiplying an entire $n \times n$ matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number to the power of $n$. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the entire matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A) &={k}^{n}\cdot det(A),\end{aligned}
$$

where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix."] ["activity-6e245c04-c2d0-5852-8dd2-a60dcd6eacc6" :activity/id #uuid "6e245c04-c2d0-5852-8dd2-a60dcd6eacc6"] ["step-025b43f4-b967-5253-bd0e-79c0a7e61eb7" :step/id "step-025b43f4-b967-5253-bd0e-79c0a7e61eb7"]] "retractions" [[17592186079646 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to calculate the following limit:

$$
\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x} - 1}{x - 1}
$$

If we try to evaluate the limit by directly substituting $x=1,$ we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\sqrt{x}-1}{x-1} & =\frac{\sqrt{1}-1}{1-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we simplify the fraction before evaluating the limit, we obtain a more clear result. To simplify the fraction, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator of the function by the **conjugate** of the numerator.

To obtain the conjugate of $\sqrt{x}-1,$ we simply switch the sign between the two terms to get $\sqrt{x}+ 1.$ 

$$
\eqalign{
\require{cancel}
\lim_{x\to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x} - 1} {x - 1}
	&= \lim_{x\to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x} - 1} {x - 1} \cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{x} + 1}{\sqrt{x} + 1}	\
	&=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac{(\sqrt{x} - 1)(\sqrt{x} +1)} {(x-1)(\sqrt{x} + 1)}\
        &=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac{\left(\sqrt{x}\right)^2 - 1^2} {(x-1)(\sqrt{x} + 1)}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac{x-1} {(x-1)(\sqrt{x} + 1)}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac{\cancel{x-1}} {\cancel{(x-1)}(\sqrt{x} + 1)}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac1{\sqrt{x} + 1}\
        &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1} +1}\
	&=\dfrac{1}{2}
}
$$"] [17592186199518 :tutorial/content "Recall that the statement "$A$ and $B$", represented symbolically as $A \land B$, is true if $A$ is true *and* $B$ is true. Otherwise, it is false.

We can represent all possible permutations of the truth values of $A$ and $B$ and the subsequent truth values of $A\land B$ using a **truth table**:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A \land B\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

Each row of the truth table contains an input for $A$, an input for $B$, and the corresponding output for $A \land B$.

- The first row says that if $A$ is true and $B$ is true, then $A \land B$ is true.
- The second row says that if $A$ is true and $B$ is false, then $A \land B$ is false.
- The third row says that if $A$ is false and $B$ is true, then $A \land B$ is false.
- The fourth row says that if $A$ is false and $B$ is false, then $A \land B$ is false."] [17592186199600 :tutorial/content "The statement "$A$ or $B$," represented symbolically as $A \lor B$, is true if $A$ is true, or $B$ is true, or both $A$ and $B$ are true. Otherwise, it is false.

The corresponding truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A \lor B\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

As we'll see, truth tables provide a convenient way to determine the truth values of complex logical statements. They can also be used to prove some mathematical theorems!"] [17592186199601 :tutorial/content "Consider the following statement:

$$
A \land (B\lor A)
$$

We can use a truth table to calculate the truth values of this statement given all possible permutations of the truth values of $A$ and $B$.

First, we complete a truth table for the part in parentheses, $B \lor A$. The statement $B \lor A$ is true if either $A$ is true, $B$ is true, or both $A$ and $B$ are true.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

Next, we add a new column for $A \land (B\lor A)$.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |

To fill in the rows, we consider the truth values of $A$ and $(B\lor A)$ and use this to determine the truth value of $A \land (B\lor A)$ in each case.

- Consider the first row. Since $A$ is true and $(B\lor A)$ is true, their conjunction $A \land (B\lor A)$ is *true*:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |

- Next, consider the second row. Since $A$ is true and $(B\lor A)$ is true, their conjunction $A \land (B\lor A)$ is *true*:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |

- Now, consider the third row. Since $A$ is false and $(B\lor A)$ is true, their conjunction $A \land (B\lor A)$ is *false*:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |

- Finally, consider the fourth row. Since $A$ is false and $(B\lor A)$ is false, their conjunction $A \land (B\lor A)$ is *false*:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |

The completed truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B \lor A\,$ | $\,A \land (B \lor A)\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |"] [17592186199519 :tutorial/content "Two statements are **logically equivalent** if they have identical truth tables.

A trivial logical equivalence is that every statement is logically equivalent to itself. We write this as follows:
$P \equiv P$

To prove this, we can use a truth table.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,P\,$ |
| --- | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

Since $P$ and $P$ have identical truth values, they're logically equivalent.

Another trivial equivalence is that the conjunction of a statement with itself is equivalent to the original statement.
$P \land P \equiv P$

For example, the compound statement "$x=3$ and $x=3$" is logically equivalent to "$x=3$", which matches our intuition.

Again, we can prove the general result using a truth table.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,P\,$ | $\,P \land P\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

The statements $P$ and $P\land P$ are logically equivalent since they have identical truth values.

We also have the following logical equivalence for the disjunction of $P$ with itself.
$P \lor P \equiv P$

We can justify this result using a truth table.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,P\,$ | $\,P \lor P\,$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |

The statements $P$ and $P\lor P$ are logically equivalent since they have identical truth values.

Collectively, the results
$P\land P \equiv P,\qquad P\lor P \equiv P$

are known as the **idempotent laws.**"] [17592186060893 :tutorial/content "The derivatives of sine, cosine, and tangent are shown in the table below:

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\sin x$ | $\cos x$ |
| $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ |
| $\tan x$ | $\sec^2 x$ |

Now that we know the derivatives of the standard trigonometric functions, we can differentiate any combination of them by using the properties of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of $y = \cos x + \sin x.$

Here, we can use the fact that the derivative of the sum is equal to the sum of the derivatives, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}x+\operatorname{sin}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}x+\operatorname{cos}x.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We'll derive the derivatives shown in the table at the end of this lesson."] [17592186060894 :tutorial/content "To understand why the derivative of sine is cosine, we need to use the definition of the derivative:

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}} {\textrm{d}x} (\sin x) =  \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\dfrac{\sin(x+h) - \sin x}{h}
$$

Now, the so-called **addition formula for sine** states that

$$
\sin(x+h) = \sin(x)\cos(h)+\cos (x)  \sin(h).
$$

By using the addition formula for sine, we can rewrite our expression for the derivative as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}(x)\operatorname{cos}(h)+\operatorname{sin}(h)\operatorname{cos}(x)-\operatorname{sin}(x)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}(x)(\operatorname{cos}(h)-1)+\operatorname{cos}(x)\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\operatorname{sin}(x)\frac{(\operatorname{cos}(h)-1)}{h}+\operatorname{cos}(x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}(x){{{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\operatorname{cos}(h)-1)}{h}}_{⏟}}_{0}+\operatorname{cos}(x){{{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h}}_{⏟}}_{1} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

In the last step, we used two important results for trigonometric limits:

$$
\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \dfrac{1 - \cos(h)}{h}=0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin(h)}{h}=1.
$$

Deriving these results requires separate discussions, which we'll leave to future topics."] [17592186060895 :tutorial/content "We can follow the same method for the cosine and use the definition of the derivative to show that $(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$ First, we start with the definition of the derivative:

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}} {\textrm{d}x} (\cos x) =  \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\dfrac{\cos(x+h) - \cos x}{h}
$$

Now, the so-called **addition formula for cosine** states that

$$
\cos(x+h) = \cos(x)\cos(h)- \sin(x)\sin(h).
$$

Using the addition formula for cosine, we can rewrite our expression for the derivative as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}(x)\operatorname{cos}(h)-\operatorname{sin}(x)\operatorname{sin}(h)-\operatorname{cos}(x)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}(x)(\operatorname{cos}(h)-1)-\operatorname{sin}(x)\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(x){{{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}(h)-1}{h}}_{⏟}}_{0}-\operatorname{sin}(x){{{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h}}_{⏟}}_{1} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Once again, in the last step, we used the special limits for sine and cosine."] [17592186060897 :tutorial/content "The **second derivative**  is the derivative of a function's first derivative. It is written as $f''(x).$

To calculate the second derivative of a function $f(x)$, we first need to calculate the first derivative $f'(x).$ After that, we calculate the derivative of $f'(x).$ So using prime $\left('\right)$ notation, we can define the second derivative of a function $f(x)$ as

$$
f''(x) = (f'(x))'.
$$

Let's try it out with the function $f(x) = 4x^2 + 3x.$ The first derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =(4{x}^{2}+3x)^{'} \\  & =4(2)x+3 \\  & =8x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the derivative of $f'(x)$ to give us $f''(x).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{''}(x) & =({f}^{'}(x))^{'} \\  & =(8x+3)^{'} \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the second derivative of $f(x)$ is $8.$"] [17592186060899 :tutorial/content "To calculate the third derivative of the function $f(x)=2x^4+3x,$ we need to differentiate it three times.

Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{4}+3x) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{4-1}+1\cdot 3{x}^{1-1} \\ \text{ } & =8{x}^{3}+3{x}^{0} \\  & =8{x}^{3}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{''}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{3}+3) \\  & =8\cdot 3{x}^{3-1}+0 \\ \text{ } & =24{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(24{x}^{2}) \\  & =24\cdot 2{x}^{2-1} \\ \text{ } & =48x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third derivative of $f(x)$ is $f'''(x)=48x.$ 

Using Leibniz notation, the third derivative of a function $f(x)$ can also be written as

$$
f'''(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(f(x))\right)\right)=\dfrac {\textrm d^3}{\textrm d x^3}f(x).
$$

In general, if we want to calculate the $n$-th order derivative of a function, we need to differentiate it $n$ times:

$$
f^{(n)}(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d^n}{\textrm d x^n}f(x).
$$

**Note**: The parenthesis in the superscript of $f^{(n)}(x)$ means that it is the the $n$-th derivative of $f(x).$ This is to distinguish it from $f^n(x)$ with no parenthesis, which indicates the $n$-th power of $f(x).$"] [17592186153426 :tutorial/content "The **negation** of a mathematical statement is its *opposite* statement. A mathematical statement and its negation have opposite truth values.

For example:

- The negation of the *true* statement "$4$ is divisible by $2$" is the *false* statement "$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$"
- The negation of the *false* statement "$5$ is even" is the *true* statement "$5$ is odd."

We can express negations using the symbol "$\neg$". The negation of $A$ is denoted $\neg A,$ and has the opposite truth values as $A{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

We can negate compound statements as well. For example, the statement $\neg (A \land B)$ has the opposite truth values as the statement $A \land B{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, \neg (A \land B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |"] [17592186153427 :tutorial/content "When we have two negations in a row, we can cancel them out.

- For example, $\neg (\neg A)$ can be simplified to $A.$
- Likewise, $\neg (\neg (A \land B))$ can be simplified to $A \land B.$

To understand why negations cancel with each other, consider the following statement:

$4$ is divisible by $2.$

The negation of this statement is

$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$

If we negate again, we get back the original sentence:

$4$ divisible by $2.$

So, if we negate a statement twice, we end up with the original statement.

More formally, we can prove that $\neg (\neg A) \equiv A$ using a truth table.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ | $\,\neg(\neg A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |

Since $A$ and $\neg(\neg A)$ have the same truth values, they are logically equivalent."] [17592186121020 :tutorial/content "Remember the following three standard elementary row operations: 

  I. Swapping two rows

  II. Multiplying a row by a non-zero number

  III. Adding a multiple of one row to another row

Of these three elementary row operations, only III (adding a multiple of one row to another row) *preserves* the determinant. The other two operations, switching two rows or multiplying a row by a non-zero number, *change* the determinant.

To demonstrate, let's consider the matrix ![](images/fa/fa51d7c585db408c47e8640ae839c1a3bbf94e2b0097e1ade511e5773461f1e8.svg) Taking the determinant, we have
![](images/bc/bcf5c5dc9f5b7ed3849e719665f802040cf51e3334ae99e25ea7648cbb0f6134.svg)

If we swap the two rows, we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4 \\  & =2 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, if we multiply top row by ${\color{red}2},$ then we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

However, if we add twice the top row to the bottom row, then we get the same determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3+2\cdot 1 & 4+2\cdot 2\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot 8-2\cdot 5 \\  & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186121061 :tutorial/content "Let's check what happens if we multiply the entire matrix (not only one row) by a number. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ |\begin{aligned}3\cdot 1 & 3\cdot 2 \\ 3\cdot 3 & 3\cdot 4\end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 9 & 12\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 12-6\cdot 9=-18\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

![](images/fe/fe02091dde43a8a2405f6b588f619bc9fa3f54b31ac8a1ac39d318761f00cc3e.svg)

The above is equivalent to multiplying both rows of the matrix by $3$. Multiplying the first row scales the determinant by $3$, and then multiplying the second row scales it by $3$ once more.

In general, multiplying an entire $n \times n$ matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number to the power of $n$. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the entire matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A),\end{aligned}
$$

where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix."]]}

" :question/worked-solution "Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: $$ x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].$ So, $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}]. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t-s} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t-s} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186229675 Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$ {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}. $$ Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\ & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186308719 :question/id We are given that $$ {e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]. $$ Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\ & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}]. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\ & ={[\begin{aligned}(-s+t+1){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\ & =[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-t}-t{e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186535950 :question/id #uuid "5cb555db-6a59-509d-947e-27c4f1a2a7e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-335062" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d4f64bf3-528b-508d-afe7-7fb41040696f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\cos(t)-1" :db/id 17592186535760}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186535760} :answer-field/id #uuid "c0cddfae-ecf5-50fd-9bfc-04c2102bb55f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186535905}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

:tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving *inhomogeneous systems* of ODEs as well. Consider the system $$ \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t), $$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, and suppose we are given an initial condition $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$. Our goal is to derive the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system. First, we eliminate the *inhomogeneous term* by a change of variables. We define $$ \mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t) $$ and differentiate it using the product rule: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\ & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\ & =\cancel{-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+\cancel{A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\ & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned} $$ Now, we integrate both sides from $t_0$ to $t$ and get $$ \mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t_0)=\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Next, since $\mathbf{y}(t_0)=e^{-A(t_0-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0),$ we have $$ \mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Finally, we convert back to the initial variable $\mathbf{x}(t).$ To do that we multiply both sides by $e^{A(t-t_0)}{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the solution to our IVP is $$ \mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where the first term represents the solution of the corresponding *homogeneous system*, and the second term gives a particular solution of our *inhomogeneous system*. Let's see some concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "ff1bfa7f-286f-5481-8170-effabae1aa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14524 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid " :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t), $$ where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: $$ x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$ {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}. $$ Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\ & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "06d91f07-0fea-5beb-aa8a-cd77b3e6a896" where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. $\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ $\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$ $\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ $\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$ $\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ $\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$ $\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$ $\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ $\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$ Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning. $\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}. $\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line {{field-2}} by substituting {{field-3}}. $\,$ Line $\text{L9}$ follows from line $\text{L7}$ by {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps. - We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from $$ {y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) $$ in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\ & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\ & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned} $$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$ - Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have $$ y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes $$ y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s, $$ so $$ y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$ - Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that $$ {e}^{At}y(t)=x(t). $$ Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into $$ {e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s $$ from $\text{L7}$ gives $$ x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$"} :step/id #uuid "2231ccca-1dd5-57de-b365-dbd0a5f43637" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495250}} {:db/id 17592186495193 :step/content {:db/id 17592186308718 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c139fc5d-402e-5c97-b048-caf60e14b36c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}(2t)-\operatorname{cos}(2t)+3" :db/id 17592186306955} {:answer/id #uuid "6963f53e-90b3-59a4-b3ac-6bc885da9965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\cos(2t)+2\sin(2t)" :db/id 17592186494533}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494533} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b933995-aeb2-5960-92c8-2edb1a0843a3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307958}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "03656a1f-f3fa-5cdf-b35f-3b5febfaad49" :question/math-academy-id "q-335054" :question/problem "$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-2x(t)+3,\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$ {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}. $$ Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\ & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. $\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ $\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$ $\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ $\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$ $\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ $\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$ $\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$ $\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ $\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$ Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning. $\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}. $\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line {{field-2}} by {{field-3}}. $\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps. - We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from $$ {y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) $$ in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\ & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\ & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned} $$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$ - Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of $$ y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds $$ from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$ - Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of $$ y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t) $$ from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-At}x(t) \\ & =x(t).\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$"} :step/id #uuid "c5aef665-a069-598d-9521-f09b9a91fe69"}] :activity/title "Solving Inhomogeneous Systems of ODEs Using Matrix Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186494314} {:db/id 17592186046660} {:db/id 17592186495193 :step/content {:db/id 17592186308718 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c139fc5d-402e-5c97-b048-caf60e14b36c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}(2t)-\operatorname{cos}(2t)+3" :db/id 17592186306955} {:answer/id #uuid "6963f53e-90b3-59a4-b3ac-6bc885da9965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\cos(2t)+2\sin(2t)" :db/id 17592186494533}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494533} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b933995-aeb2-5960-92c8-2edb1a0843a3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307958}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "03656a1f-f3fa-5cdf-b35f-3b5febfaad49" :question/math-academy-id "q-335054" :question/problem "$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-2x(t)+3,\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$ {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}. $$ Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\ & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\
