" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t), $$ where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: $$ x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$ {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}. $$ Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\ & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "2fbeaf38-2336-5aee-bfc1-de7e502565a2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495181}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid our system in matrix form, we get $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t), $$ where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: $$ x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$ {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}. $$ Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\ & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\ & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\ & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned} $$ Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$ - Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have $$ y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes $$ y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s, $$ so $$ y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$ - Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$, $\text{L8}$, and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that $$ {e}^{At}y(t)=x(t). $$ Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into $$ {e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s $$ from $\text{L7}$ gives $$ x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$"} :step/id #uuid "7a5de0ff-7990-5b8c-9f62-a36d2977e2f1"} {:db/id 17592186536036 :step/content {:db/id 17592186535950 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d4f64bf3-528b-508d-afe7-7fb41040696f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\cos(t)-1" :db/id 17592186535760}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186535760} :answer-field/id #uuid "c0cddfae-ecf5-50fd-9bfc-04c2102bb55f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186535905}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5cb555db-6a59-509d-947e-27c4f1a2a7e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-335062" :question/problem "$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get $$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t), $$ where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$ Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: $$ x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$ {e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]. $$ Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\ & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that $$ {e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]. $$ So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\ & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\ & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "98ff146f-1e74-5987-92d5-7e14960c7748" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536026}} {:db/id at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$ To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\ & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\ & =3\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=3x-3\end{aligned}\right. $$"} {:db/id 17592186268883 :question/id #uuid "484f8b36-97b4-5e4f-a875-d05f61c48bf6" point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1 \\ z &=-3y-1\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,-3,-1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =j-3\,k\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j-3\,k.$"} {:db/id 17592186268891 :question/id #uuid "7da12630-1fa6-595d-a465-5095a1603e7f" :question/math-academy-id "q-132599"} the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,1).$ To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =2(1+1)-2=2\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(1,1) & ={f}_{x}(1,1)(x-1) \\ z-1 & =2(x-1) \\ z-1 & =2x-2 \\ z & =2x-1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=2x-1\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=2x-1$ (or $2x-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨2,0,-1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨2,0,-1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =-i-2\,k\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since $-i-2\,k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-2\,k)=i+2\,k$ is also parallel to it."} {:db/id the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,-6).$ To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,-6):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,-6) & =\frac{-6-(-2)}{\sqrt{(-2)(-6+(-2))}} \\ & =\frac{-4}{\sqrt{16}} \\ & =-\frac{4}{4} \\ & =-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(-2,-6) & ={f}_{y}(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\ z-1 & =-1(y+6) \\ z-1 & =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,-6,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-2 \\ z &=-y-5\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =-j+k \\ & =⟨0,-1,1⟩\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1) \\ & =2\cdot 1-0 \\ & =2\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & ={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1)(y-1) \\ z-0 & =2(y-1) \\ z & =2y-2\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z &=2y-2\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =j+2\,k \\ & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$"} {:db/id 17592186385494 :question/id #uuid "851f656d-69a9-5c8d-8482-1385f4b7fe8a" line to the function, the partial derivative of a function has a geometric interpretation as well. To illustrate, consider the surface $z = f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2$ and the plane $x=3.$ The intersection of the surface and the plane forms a downward parabolic curve, as shown below. A point $P(3,2,5)$ is plotted and a tangent line is drawn through that point. ![](images/86/8619c41cd0caf04ae9ee9bcae61e31739d8da583793a67c1c87e00186c3ac417.png) To find the slope of the tangent, we can compute the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5)\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(18-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\ & =-2y \\ {\frac{∂f}{∂y}|}_{P} & =-2(2) \\ & =-4\end{aligned} $$ **Note:** To verify that this result is correct, we can find the equation of the downward parabolic curve and then use single-variable calculus to compute the slope of the tangent line. To find the equation of the downward parabolic curve, we can substitute the equation of the plane ($x=3$) into the equation of the surface ($f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2$). Doing this, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(3,y) & =18-{3}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\ & =9-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ So, the equation of the downward parabolic curve is $z=g(y) = 9-y^2.$ In the $yz$-plane, this curve has the following graph: ![](images/e9/e982ef5d6d8d4fec9c64957d46f22cea2a85bd002595642f58700cf48cce4256.png) To find the slope of the tangent to $g(y)$ at $P,$ we can use single-variable calculus. We differentiate $g(y)$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5).$ This gives $$ \begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(y) & =-2y \\ {g}^{′}(2) & =-2(2) \\ & =-4.\,✓\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid that the point $P(-2,-6,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{y-x}{\sqrt{x(y+x)}}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,-6).$ To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,-6):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,-6) & =\frac{-6-(-2)}{\sqrt{(-2)(-6+(-2))}} \\ & =\frac{-4}{\sqrt{16}} \\ & =-\frac{4}{4} \\ & =-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(-2,-6) & ={f}_{y}(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\ z-1 & =-1(y+6) \\ z-1 & =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,-6,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-2 \\ z &=-y-5\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =-j+k \\ & =⟨0,-1,1⟩\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-1,1⟩.$"} :step/id #uuid "1cff8fcf-d3d9-54eb-b0e4-27eb94529c2d" :step/next {:db/id "320a3cd2-acfa-559d-b91b-9bfb6f0a3cde" :question/math-academy-id "q-71231" :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\ & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & =1\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}y &=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z &=x-1\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =-i-k \\ & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it."} :step/id #uuid =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,-6,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-2 \\ z &=-y-5\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $y=5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(4,5).$ To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(4,5):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,5) & =\frac{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}{2(4)-(5)} \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{9}}{3} \\ & =\frac{3}{3} \\ & =1\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(4,5) & ={f}_{x}(4,5)(x-4) \\ z-(-2) & =1(x-4) \\ z+2 & =x-4 \\ z & =x-6\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}y &=5 \\ z &=x-6\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $y=5,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=x-6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =-i-k\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it."} :step/id #uuid "a385dd67-f4d9-5c4e-9dcb-07bacb547fb1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186425124}} {:db/id 17592186425124 & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =-i-k\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it."} :step/id #uuid z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(0,1).$ To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(0,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & ={0}^{2}+{1}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\ & =0+1-0 \\ & =1\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-7 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+7\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,7)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=x+7\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=x+7$ (or $x-z+7=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =-i-\,k \\ & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it."} we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(0,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & ={0}^{2}+{1}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\ & =0+1-0 \\ & =1\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-7 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+7\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,7)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=x+7\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=x+7$ (or $x-z+7=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =-i-\,k \\ & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it."} :step/id #uuid "c6cce728-296b-55fc-b12d-c3661e00af21"} {:db/id 17592186500430 :step/content $(\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =2(\frac{1}{2}){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi /2)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ & ={e}^{0}+1 \\ & =2\end{aligned} $$ the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,2).$ To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,2):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\ & =8-4-2 \\ & =2\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: $$ \begin{aligned}z-f(-2,2) & ={f}_{y}(-2,2)(y-2) \\ z-3 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-2 \\ z &=2y-1\end{aligned}\right. $$ Next, notice that: - For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$ - For the plane $z=2y-1$ (or $2y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$ Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\ & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\ & =j+2\,k\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j+2\,k.$"} :step/id #uuid "a34f7fed-6748-57b7-896d-3a0ab90523d6"} {:db/id the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{(8q)^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8|\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot |q|}\end{aligned} $$ Lastly, we are told that $q>0,$ so we have $|q|=q.$ Therefore, the final answer is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot q} & = \\ \frac{3}{8q}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186542226 :question/id #uuid "f043c885-cf65-5aa1-b5b8-12a5b94bca34" :question/math-academy-id "q-152384" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3d11c2d2-3001-5e8a-be3a-e32230076db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186541553} {:answer/id #uuid "98d13ba9-dfd3-52c2-b70f-fb7735e5b240" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4z" :db/id 17592186541740} {:answer/id #uuid "a852ddcc-f65d-5be4-bb4e-4120b2627298" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186541768} {:answer/id #uuid "bf0b0421-5aec-5d9c-a383-f76749bb0f15" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{z}" :db/id 17592186541824} {:answer/id #uuid "f8c3f8b1-179e-5104-b995-51741f073176" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2z" :db/id 17592186541941}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541941} :answer-field/id #uuid "18f8115a-b5d4-5929-a1c8-36a6a9737a96" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186541976}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Simplify $\frac{\sqrt{32{z}^{5}}}{\sqrt{8{z}^{3}}}$ given that $z>0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring the quotient under a single radical and then simplify the result: $$ \frac{\sqrt{32{z}^{5}}}{\sqrt{8{z}^{3}}}=\sqrt{\frac{32{z}^{5}}{8{z}^{3}}}=\sqrt{4{z}^{2}} $$ Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. Given that this equation has no solution, what is the value of $p?$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have an equation of the form $$ ax=b $$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants, and $b\ne 0.$ If $a=0,$ then the equation has no solution. First, we rewrite the equation in the form $ax=b.$ We start by subtracting $3x$ from both sides of the equation: $$ \begin{aligned}2px & =3x+5 \\ 2px-3x & =3x+5-3x \\ 2px-3x & =5\end{aligned} $$ Next, we factor $x$ on the left-hand side. This gives $$ (2p-3)x=5. $$ Notice that this equation is now in the form $ax=b:$ $$ {{(2p-3)}_{⏟}}_{a}x={{5}_{⏟}}_{b} $$ Therefore, the equation has no solution if $$ 2p-3=0. $$ Solving this for $p,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}2p-3 & =0 \\ 2p-3+3 & =0+3 \\ 2p & =3 \\ \frac{2p}{2} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ p & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186204599 :question/id #uuid \begin{aligned}{x}^{7} & =-\frac{1}{128} \\ \sqrt[7]{{x}^{7}} & =\sqrt[7]{(-\frac{1}{128})} \\ x & =\sqrt[7]{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{7}} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the solution is $x=-\frac{1}{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "d915e072-457e-5546-ab5a-73371243b5c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186563767}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "097ae540-a1c3-563f-958f-879f687d07c8" :tutorial/content "Sometimes we know the total change in a quantity and want to find how much the quantity changes during each equal time period. In these situations, we use division. For example, suppose a total of $\[math]24$ is withdrawn from a bank account over $6$ days in equal amounts. Since money is withdrawn, the total change in the balance is $-\[/math]24$. To find the change each day, we divide the total change by the number of days: $$ -24 \div 6 $$ Evaluating the quotient, we get $$ -24 \div 6 = -4. $$ Therefore, the balance changes by $-\[math]4$ each day." :tutorial/id #uuid "2472ba13-0b69-56f2-a477-ea1b2a6fc7e3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15182 :tutorial/title "Solving Problems Using Division of Rational Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "f88bb973-cdd9-5dc3-a6f0-ee3f3807638e" :step/math-academy-id 621978 :step/next {:db/id 17592186502176}} {:db/id 17592186502210 :step/content {:db/id 17592186502069 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186502120 :question/id #uuid "7be163d0-2103-5467-9bba-a4090855cc8b" :question/math-academy-id "e-22729"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f589fffd-f5c4-590e-9ed1-01c20390700f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186502092} {:db/id 17592186502119}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Problems Involving Multiplying Negative Fractions and Mixed Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "f8abbf23-8275-57f4-b19a-767b1595b9d0" :step/math-academy-id 621944 :step/next {:db/id 17592186502209}}] :activity/title "Solving Problems Using Multiplication and Division of Rational Numbers" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186092407} {:db/id 17592186502186 :step/content {:db/id 17592186502216 :tutorial/content "Some real-world situations involve a quantity changing by the same amount repeatedly. What is the measure of each interior angle? Recall that the sum of the interior angles of a polygon with $n$ sides equals $180^\circ \cdot (n-2).$ All interior angles in a regular polygon are congruent. So, to calculate the measure of each interior angle, we find the sum of the interior angles and divide by the number of angles. A pentagon has $n=5$ sides. Therefore, the sum of its interior angles is $$ 180^\circ \times (5 - 2) = 540^\circ. $$ Therefore, the measure of each interior angle is $$ \dfrac{540^\circ}{5} = 108^\circ, $$ as shown below. $a$ and $b$ are constants, and - $b$ is *not* equal to zero, which we write as $b \neq 0.$ Then, if $a = 0,$ the equation has **no solutions.** Indeed, by substituting $a = 0$ into $ax=b,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}ax & =b \\ (0)x & =b \\ 0 & =b\end{aligned} $$ which is a *contradiction* (i.e., a statement that's always false) because we were told that $b \neq 0.$ Therefore, the equation has no solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a5cc3be-1b56-5e46-8944-f75697b65b59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13428 :tutorial/title "Conditions for an Equation To Have No Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "a4d784bb-4dc8-51b7-9c57-1caf81eeaf95" :step/math-academy-id 476521 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205038}} {:db/id 17592186205038 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205207 :tutorial/content "Consider the equation in the variable $x,$ given by $$ 7qx = -5, $$ where $q$ is a constant. Given that this equation has no solutions, what is the value of $q?$ Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = b{:}$ $$ \underbrace{7q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{-5}_{\large b} $$ In this case, $$ a = 7q, \qquad b = -5. $$ We know that an equation of the form $ax=b$ with $b \neq 0$ has no solutions when $a = 0.$ Therefore, the equation has no solution if $$ 7q = 0. $$ Solving this for $q,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}7q & =0 \\ \frac{7q}{7} & =\frac{0}{7} \\ q & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that the equation $7qx = -5$ has no solutions if $q = 0.$ **Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "d31382b3-ae61-5a9e-a3bf-53f71f939a5d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13402 :tutorial/title "Problems Involving Unknown :question/worked-solution "First, we note that - $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero - $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows $$ \frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c} $$ The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero. Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows: $$ \frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4} $$ Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows: $$ \frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4} $$ We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: $$ \begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "04bd31c0-ddc2-5b9c-ad07-d73251e35927" :step/next {:db/id 17592186540140}} {:db/id 17592186540123 :step/content {:db/id 17592186540100 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d56b3b6-d2ee-5a6a-ac79-f166c602aad7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186539536} {:answer/id #uuid "5bbc6a18-26ef-5ee7-a216-046a93109cdd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186539634} {:answer/id #uuid "684d8919-d630-53ec-be88-da83985b9cfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186539650} {:answer/id #uuid "adf72623-7732-5460-b0b6-5cc1011adb27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{6}" :db/id 17592186539775} {:answer/id #uuid "f71975b1-e674-5e94-a227-f47c16e02797" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/id 17592186539894}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539894} :answer-field/id #uuid "746714c2-cc0f-5a43-9606-b934d8793273" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539966}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "dba16e2f-f755-5c6f-b25b-801d348b9282" :question/math-academy-id "q-67435" :question/problem "Solve the equation $-\frac{4}{x-2}=\frac{1}{x-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that - value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=y-{x}^{2}=0.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system: $$ ∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=0 $$ We start by solving the first equation: $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨-2x,1⟩\end{aligned} $$ Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2 &=-2\lambda x \\ 1 &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-\frac{1}{\lambda } \\ \lambda &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned} $$ We can now use $\lambda $ to find $x,$ as follows: $$ x=-\frac{1}{1}=-1. $$ Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ into the condition $g(x,y)=0$ and solve for $y,$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}y-(-1)^{2} & =0 \\ y-1 & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $f$ has a possible extreme value at the point $$ (-1,1). $$ Since the given parabola opens upwards, there isn't a maximum value of $f$ on the parabola. Thus, the extreme value is the minimum of $f$ on the parabola. We evaluate $f$ at this point: | $\,(x,y)\,$ | $\,(-1,1)\,$ | | --- | --- | | $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $\,-1\,$ | Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-1,1),$ and its minimum value is $-1.$"} Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system: $$ ∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=13 $$ We start by solving the first equation: $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2,3⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned} $$ Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. :topic/math-academy-id 1948} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125553 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125845 :tutorial/content "Suppose we would like to find the minimum and maximum values of the function $$ f(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2 $$ subject to constraint $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2=1.$ In other words, we wish to find the global extrema of $f(x,y)$ defined on the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown below. ![](images/39/39893af9755488d142116370d451b7a3d92b334c27f983eb302492b0d516c41c.png) First, let's draw our constraint circle ($x^2+y^2=1$) and consider the level curves of $f(x,y).$ These level curves are ellipses of the form $$ f(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2 = k. $$ As we increase the parameter $k,$ we get ellipses with larger and larger axes, as shown below. ![](images/d5/d59d566c9cf7e252884a1397eb4ac0c8f85b290790e9063be2ff6eb4a4aff04a.png) As we continue to increase $k,$ a level curve will touch the circle at the points $(\pm 1, 0)$ for some value of $k.$ The value of $k$ corresponding to that level curve gives us the *smallest* possible value of $f(x,y)$ on our circle $x^2+y^2=1.$ Increasing $k$ even further, we'll get another value of $k$ for which the corresponding level curve touches the circle at the points $(0, \pm 1),$ as shown below. This value of $k$ gives us the *largest* possible value of the function $f(x,y)$ on our circle. ![](images/48/48f71f5aa237936be24ccba572fb650b0d477c252d8338549a33cfea4874cbad.png) Notice that the corresponding level curves touch the circle in both cases (the minimum and the maximum). So, the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ and the circle $g(x,y)=1$ have a common tangent at these points. This means that the *gradients* of both curves must be parallel at these points. Therefore, at the extreme points, we must have $$ \nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), $$ where $\lambda$ is some real number. The number $\lambda$ is called a **Lagrange multiplier**. We can now use these observations to write down a general method for optimizing a function subject to a constraint." :tutorial/id #uuid "932667c3-77f7-56cb-ae08-dd6835e29462" :tutorial/math-academy-id Lagrange multipliers** states that the extrema of a function $f(x,y)$ subject to constraint $g(x,y)=c$ can be found by solving the system $$ \nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=c. $$ The method of Lagrange multipliers assumes that $\nabla g \neq \mathbf{0}$ on the curve $g(x,y)=c.$ Note that solutions to this system do not always exist! For example, the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ does not have a minimum (or maximum) on the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=1.$ However, we can use the following theorem to guarantee the existence of solutions in some cases: *If $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint function $g(x,y) = c$ is closed and bounded, then $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "906426bb-122c-5b43-a304-d63921ab20dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7750 :tutorial/title "The Method of Lagrange Multipliers"} :step/id #uuid "0d14ea94-0983-5096-b7d2-ed0dc8de4dce" :step/math-academy-id 44868 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125660}} {:db/id 17592186125660 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125894 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider our previous example, where we wish to find the extrema of the function $f(x,y)=2x^2+4y^2$ on the circle $g(x,y)=x^2+y^2=1.$ The method of Lagrange multipliers states that we need to solve the following system: $$ \nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=c $$ We start by solving the first equation: $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}4x &=2\lambda x \\ 8y &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(2-\lambda ) &=0 \\ y(4-\lambda ) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned} $$ To solve this system, we break it up into several cases: - Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies $$ \begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,y=\pm 1.\end{aligned} $$ This gives the critical points $\left(0,\pm 1 \right).$ - Assuming $\lambda =2$ in the first equation, the second equation implies $$ \begin{aligned}y(4-2)=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned} $$ Then, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,x=\pm 1.\end{aligned} $$ This gives the critical points $\left(\pm 1, 0 \right).$ Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points $$ (\pm 1, 0), \qquad (0, \pm1). $$ Finally, we evaluate $f$ at these points: | $(x,y)$ | $(\pm 1,0)$ | $(0, \pm 1)$ | | --- | --- | --- | | $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $4$ | Therefore, the function reaches a minimum of $2$ at the points $(\pm 1, 0)$ and a maximum of $4$ at points $(0, \pm 1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid :tutorial/content "The **method of Lagrange multipliers** states that the extrema of a function $f(x,y)$ subject to constraint $g(x,y)=c$ can be found by solving the system $$ \nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=c. $$ The method of Lagrange multipliers assumes that $\nabla g \neq \mathbf{0}$ on the curve $g(x,y)=c.$ Note that solutions to this system do not always exist! For example, the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ does not have a minimum (or maximum) on the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=1.$ However, we can use the following theorem to guarantee the existence of solutions in some cases: *If $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint function $g(x,y) = c$ is closed and bounded, then $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "906426bb-122c-5b43-a304-d63921ab20dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7750 :tutorial/title "The Method of Lagrange Multipliers"} {:db/id 17592186125660 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125894 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider our previous example, where we wish to find the extrema of the function $f(x,y)=2x^2+4y^2$ on the circle $g(x,y)=x^2+y^2=1.$ The method of Lagrange multipliers states that we need to solve the following system: $$ \nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=c $$ We start by solving the first equation: $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}4x &=2\lambda x \\ 8y &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(2-\lambda ) &=0 \\ y(4-\lambda ) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned} $$ To solve this system, we break it up into several cases: - Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies $$ \begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,y=\pm 1.\end{aligned} $$ This gives the critical points $\left(0,\pm 1 \right).$ - Assuming $\lambda =2$ in the first equation, the second equation implies $$ \begin{aligned}y(4-2)=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned} $$ Then, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,x=\pm 1.\end{aligned} $$ This gives the critical points $\left(\pm 1, 0 \right).$ Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points $$ (\pm 1, 0), \qquad (0, \pm1). $$ Finally, we evaluate $f$ at these points: | $(x,y)$ | $(\pm 1,0)$ | $(0, \pm 1)$ | | --- | --- | --- | | $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $4$ | Therefore, the function reaches a minimum of $2$ at the points $(\pm 1, 0)$ and a maximum of $4$ at points $(0, \pm 1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a5ffe247-960a-5ed1-92ae-ae8c917cbefc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7881 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id {x^2-\left(2\sqrt{x}\right)^2} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \ &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x^2-4x} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \ &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x(x-4)} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \ &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} $$ If we try to evaluate the limit by directly substituting $x=1,$ we get an indeterminate form: $$ \begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\sqrt{x}-1}{x-1} & =\frac{\sqrt{1}-1}{1-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned} $$ However, if we simplify the fraction before evaluating the limit, we obtain a more clear result. To simplify the fraction, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator of the function by the **conjugate** of the numerator. To obtain the conjugate of $\sqrt{x}-1,$ we simply switch the sign between the two terms to get $\sqrt{x}+ 1.$ $$ \eqalign{ \require{cancel} \lim_{x\to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x} - 1} {x - 1} &= \lim_{x\to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x} - 1} {x - 1} \cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{x} + 1}{\sqrt{x} + 1} \ &=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac{(\sqrt{x} - 1)(\sqrt{x} +1)} {(x-1)(\sqrt{x} + 1)}\ &=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac{\left(\sqrt{x}\right)^2 - 1^2} {(x-1)(\sqrt{x} + 1)}\ &=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac{x-1} {(x-1)(\sqrt{x} + 1)}\ &=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac{\cancel{x-1}} {\cancel{(x-1)}(\sqrt{x} + 1)}\ &=\lim_{x\to 1} \dfrac1{\sqrt{x} + 1}\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1} +1}\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} } $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "73481739-fdce-5a28-84e1-5145ea62af87" :tutorial/math-academy-id 250 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the following system consisting of the equations of the curves: $$ \{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+x+4 \\ y=5x\end{aligned} $$ Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x+4 & =5x \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned} $$ So, the $x$-coordinate of the intersection point is $x=2.$ To find the $y$-coordinate of the intersection point, we plug this value into either curve. Let's choose the equation of the line. {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that the line $y=x+k$ does **not** intersect the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1,$ what is the range of possible values of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "To determine whether the line $y=x+k$ intersects the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1,$ we need to solve the following system of equations for the two curves: $$ \{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+1 \\ y=x+k\end{aligned} $$ Setting the equations equal to one another and writing in standard form, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & =x+k \\ {x}^{2}-x+1-k & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we solve this equation using the quadratic formula with $a=1,\,b=-1,$ and $c=1-k:$ $$ \begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-(-1)\pm \sqrt{(-1)^{2}-4(1)(1-k)}}{2(1)} \\ & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{1-4+4k}}{2} \\ & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{4k-3}}{2}\end{aligned} $$ Since the line and parabola do not intersect, our quadratic equation must have no real solutions; hence, the expression inside the square root must be negative. Setting up and solving this inequality, we get $$ \begin{aligned}4k-3 & <0 \\ 4k & <3 \\ k & <\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the range of possible values of $k$ is $k<\frac{3}{4}.$"} {:db/id 17592186048490} {:db/id 17592186048559} {:db/id 17592186048779} {:db/id 17592186049119} {:db/id 17592186049231} {:db/id 17592186049275} {:db/id 17592186049446} {:db/id 17592186049770} {:db/id 17592186050022} {:db/id 17592186051028} {:activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186217980} :activity/id #uuid "f67186a8-3fe3-5bdd-b09e-4edfe15e8cef" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049837 :topic/id #uuid "17cac727-fab1-5837-8069-a3e9364662a5" :topic/math-academy-id 6341} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186217980 :step/content {:db/id 17592186218320 :tutorial/content "Consider the line $y = x + 2$ and the parabola $y = x^2 + x + 1,$ shown in the graph below. ![](images/9d/9d7ca10163c9b5096f90e19bdb50d98881bd55e92cbaea4aa5af6696e728f9f3.png) We can see from the diagram that there are two points of intersection. So let's calculate the coordinates of these intersection points. An intersection point is a common solution of the equations $y = x + 2$ and $y = x^2 + x + 1.$ In other words, to get the coordinates of the intersection points, we have to solve the following system of equations: $$ \{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+x+1 \\ y=x+2\end{aligned} $$ Setting the equations equal to one another and then solving for $x$ using our knowledge of quadratic equations, we get ![](images/96/9618f0221da97c281424def31e5d2a8fb96422b800928ad4ec4a01ed4dbad3d7.svg) So, the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. we get $$ \begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\ & =(1)+2 \\ & =3,\end{aligned} $$ so the other point of intersection is $(1,3).$ Therefore, we conclude that the points of intersection are $\left(-1,\,1 \right)$ standard form, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & =x+k \\ {x}^{2}-x+1-k & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we solve this equation using the quadratic formula with $a=1,\,b=-1,$ and $c=1-k:$ $$ \begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-(-1)\pm \sqrt{(-1)^{2}-4(1)(1-k)}}{2(1)} \\ & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{1-4+4k}}{2} \\ & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{4k-3}}{2}\end{aligned} $$ Since the line and parabola do not intersect, our quadratic equation must have no real solutions; hence, the expression inside the square root must be negative. Setting up and solving this inequality, we get $$ \begin{aligned}4k-3 & <0 \\ 4k & <3 \\ k & <\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the range of possible values of $k$ is $k<\frac{3}{4}.$"} :step/id For instance, the speed of sound is approximately $0.34$ kilometers per second. What is this in meters per second? We can find out using the following two steps. ** Step 1: Create a conversion formula.** We are given the units $\dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{s}},$ and we want to convert this into $\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}.$ To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us: $$ \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{s}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}} $$ We want to replace $\textrm{km}$ with $\textrm{m}.$ To get rid of $\textrm{km},$ we can put $\textrm{km}$ in the denominator so that it cancels out: $$ \require{cancel} \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}} }{s}\cdot \dfrac{?}{\cancel{ \textrm{km} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}} $$ Then, to introduce $\textrm{m},$ we can put $\textrm{m}$ in the numerator: $$ \require{cancel} \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}} }{s}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m} }{\cancel{ \textrm{km} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}} $$ So, our conversion formula is $$ \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{s}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m} }{\textrm{km} } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}. $$ **Step 2: Use the conversion formula.** Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it. - The speed that we wish to convert is $0.34 \, \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{s}}.$ - There are $1\,000$ meters per kilometer. Applying our conversion formula, we have $$ \begin{aligned}0.34\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{s}} & =0.34\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{s}}\cdot 1\,000\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{km}} \\ & =(0.34\cdot 1\,000)\,\frac{\cancel{\text{km}}}{\text{s}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{km}}} \\ & =340\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the speed of sound is $340$ meters per second." definition of the derivative: $$ \dfrac {\textrm{d}} {\textrm{d}x} (\sin x) = \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\dfrac{\sin(x+h) - \sin x}{h} $$ Now, the so-called **addition formula for sine** states that $$ \sin(x+h) = \sin(x)\cos(h)+\cos (x) \sin(h). $$ By using the addition formula for sine, we can rewrite our expression for the derivative as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}(x)\operatorname{cos}(h)+\operatorname{sin}(h)\operatorname{cos}(x)-\operatorname{sin}(x)}{h} \\ & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}(x)(\operatorname{cos}(h)-1)+\operatorname{cos}(x)\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h} \\ & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\operatorname{sin}(x)\frac{(\operatorname{cos}(h)-1)}{h}+\operatorname{cos}(x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h}) \\ & =\operatorname{sin}(x){{{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\operatorname{cos}(h)-1)}{h}}_{⏟}}_{0}+\operatorname{cos}(x){{{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h}}_{⏟}}_{1} \\ & =\operatorname{cos}(x)\end{aligned} $$ In the last step, we used two important results for trigonometric limits: $$ \lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \dfrac{1 - \cos(h)}{h}=0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin(h)}{h}=1. $$ Deriving these results requires separate discussions, which we'll leave to future topics." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a25dc2a-846b-5554-9cc7-682b81f17e0f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2619 :tutorial/title "Justifying the Formula for the :tutorial/content "We can follow the same method for the cosine and use the definition of the derivative to show that $(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$ First, we start with the definition of the derivative: $$ \dfrac {\textrm{d}} {\textrm{d}x} (\cos x) = \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\dfrac{\cos(x+h) - \cos x}{h} $$ Now, the so-called **addition formula for cosine** states that $$ \cos(x+h) = \cos(x)\cos(h)- \sin(x)\sin(h). $$ Using the addition formula for cosine, we can rewrite our expression for the derivative as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}(x)\operatorname{cos}(h)-\operatorname{sin}(x)\operatorname{sin}(h)-\operatorname{cos}(x)}{h} \\ & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}(x)(\operatorname{cos}(h)-1)-\operatorname{sin}(x)\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h} \\ & =\operatorname{cos}(x){{{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}(h)-1}{h}}_{⏟}}_{0}-\operatorname{sin}(x){{{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}(h)}{h}}_{⏟}}_{1} \\ & =-\operatorname{sin}(x)\end{aligned} $$ Once again, in the last step, we used the special limits for sine and cosine." :tutorial/id #uuid "40bcba62-6d88-5cfd-9d89-e773514e5a63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2620 :tutorial/title "Justifying the Formula for the Derivative of For example, let's find the derivative of $y = \cos x + \sin x.$ Here, we can use the fact that the derivative of the sum is equal to the sum of the derivatives, and get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}x+\operatorname{sin}x) \\ & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}x) \\ & =-\operatorname{sin}x+\operatorname{cos}x.\end{aligned} $$ **Note:** We'll derive the derivatives shown in the table at the end of this lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "dca4e1b4-5f89-5c88-9f24-b4671410d644" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2618 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "970c03a9-20ec-54a6-81c1-0b04852bff2d" :step/math-academy-id 12320 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060529}} {:db/id 17592186060893 :tutorial/content "The derivatives of sine, cosine, and tangent are shown in the table below: | $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | | --- | --- | | $\sin x$ | $\cos x$ | | $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ | | $\tan x$ | $\sec^2 x$ | Now that we know the derivatives of the standard trigonometric functions, we can differentiate any combination of them by using the properties of differentiation. For example, consider the function $f(x)$ whose graph is shown below. This function has a vertical asymptote at $x=1,$ and the function value $f(x)$ grows without bound as $x$ approaches the asymptote $x=1.$ What is the limit $\lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x)$? ![](images/ab/ab9d57d3952fe0221616f9e64e1295fd0511703bdd5ed3a5fe91113cc7c8bf1b.png) Remember that in order for computing any limit, in this case, $\lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x),$ we have to compute the left and right-sided limits separately and ensure that they match up. - **Left-sided limit:** As we approach $x=1$ (the vertical asymptote) from the left side of the graph, the function $f(x)$ increases without bound, approaching $\infty.$ We conclude that $$ \lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \infty. $$ - **Right-sided limit:** Likewise, as we approach the vertical asymptote $x=1$ from the right side of the graph, $f(x)$ still approaches $\infty.$ Consequently, $$ \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+ } f(x) = \infty. $$ We see that both the left and right limits exist and are equal to $\infty\mathbin{:}$ $$ \lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+} f(x) = \infty $$ As a result, the overall limit is also equal to $\infty\mathbin{:}$ $$ \lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x) = \infty $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6db8e507-0d4f-555c-b39b-e6a52ace2cd9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 156 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8d9bad47-bf42-52f0-a4a8-b5dbad51af8c" :step/math-academy-id :question/problem "If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{-t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that $$ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t). $$ First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\ & =2x\,i+2y\,j\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y={e}^{-t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})\,j \\ & ={e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, applying the chain rule, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\ & =(2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j) \\ & =2{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-t} \\ & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186125249 :question/id #uuid "72c45146-95bd-53af-b2f0-49b5ef23b12e" :question/math-academy-id $$ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t). $$ First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,k \\ & =-yz\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+z\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,k\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y={e}^{t},$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\ & =2t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, applying the chain rule, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\ & =(-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}\,i+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\,k)\cdot (2t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\ & =-2t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{t}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{t} \\ & =-2t{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}+2{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2} \\ & =2{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}-t\operatorname{sin}⁡{t}^{2}).\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186360579 :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule. The chain rule in vector form states that $$ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t). $$ First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\ & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the chain rule, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\ & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\ & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\ & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi \\ & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned} $$"} =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,j \\ & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j \\ & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\ & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the chain rule, we get $$ the function $$ f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2, $$ which takes a vector-valued function $$ \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle $$ as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$ To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t). $$ Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\ & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\ & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\ & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, applying the chain rule, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\ & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ & =-{sin}^{3}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before: $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) $$ How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that $$ \dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} = \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t} + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}? $$ Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned} $$ and $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Then $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\ & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ They are exactly the same, just different notations! **Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\ & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "15062cce-eede-545a-ae5d-e02432a0ba33" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4968 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Vector Form of the Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "fd19c878-fabf-5b99-9507-9a32fb862324" :step/math-academy-id 30937}] :activity/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule in Vector Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124728} {:db/id 17592186125528 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125835 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the function $$ f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2, $$ which takes a vector-valued function $$ \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle $$ as input. "4850b0cc-54ab-5a26-9440-b0d1cf757680" :step/math-academy-id 30936 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125319}} {:db/id 17592186125530 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125836 :tutorial/content "The chain rule for a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before: $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) $$ How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that $$ \dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} = \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t} + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}? $$ Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned} $$ and $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Then $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\ & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ They are exactly the same, just different notations! **Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\ & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "15062cce-eede-545a-ae5d-e02432a0ba33" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4968 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Vector Form of the Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "fd19c878-fabf-5b99-9507-9a32fb862324" :step/math-academy-id 30937} {:db/id 17592186125835 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the function $$ f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2, $$ which takes a vector-valued function $$ \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle $$ as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$ To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t). $$ Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\ & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\ & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\ & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, applying the chain rule, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\ & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ & =-{sin}^{3}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "673ff670-99f1-5416-aa83-5c4c8bf0e4f7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4967 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125836 :tutorial/content "The chain rule for a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before: $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) $$ How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that $$ \dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} = \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t} + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}? $$ Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned} $$ and $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Then $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\ & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$ They are exactly the same, just different notations! **Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\ & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "530f5767-4f31-5ef7-a6dd-bdeac420a724" :question/math-academy-id "q-94891" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨t-1,3,2t⟩$ at the point $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule. The chain rule in vector form states that $$ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t). $$ First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute $x=t-1,$ $y=3$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{2(t-1)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(3)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(2t)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}}⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),2t⟩ \\ & =⟨1,0,2⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the chain rule, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\ & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,2⟩ \\ & =\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 1+\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 0+\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 2 \\ & =\frac{2t-2+8t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10} \\ & =\frac{10t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=0$ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =\frac{10(0)-2}{5(0)^{2}-2(0)+10} \\ & =\frac{-2}{10} \\ & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "2989f12e-e4d2-5eea-a076-313f05f3b144" "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule. The chain rule in vector form states that $$ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t). $$ First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute $x=t-1,$ $y=3$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{2(t-1)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(3)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(2t)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}}⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),2t⟩ \\ & =⟨1,0,2⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the chain rule, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\ & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,2⟩ \\ & =\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 1+\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 0+\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 2 \\ & =\frac{2t-2+8t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10} \\ & =\frac{10t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=0$ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =\frac{10(0)-2}{5(0)^{2}-2(0)+10} \\ & =\frac{-2}{10} \\ & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "2989f12e-e4d2-5eea-a076-313f05f3b144" the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule. The chain rule in vector form states that $$ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t). $$ First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\ & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the chain rule, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\ & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\ & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\ & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi \\ & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned} $$"}
